guides.title: AI scams in India: how to spot them and what to do
guides.summary: Criminals now use AI to copy voices, faces and official-looking messages. Learn the common tricks, the simple checks, and where to report in India.

stats.label: Money lost to cyber fraud in India in 2025, from 28.15 lakh reported cases
stats.source: Ministry of Home Affairs (I4C) data, reported by ThePrint on 21 February 2026

stats.label: Money lost in 'digital arrest' scams in 2025, across 17,264 cases
stats.source: I4C data, reported by ThePrint on 18 February 2026

stats.label: Money saved after people reported fraud quickly, in more than 32.80 lakh complaints up to 30 June 2026
stats.source: Ministry of Home Affairs reply in the Lok Sabha, reported by The Free Press Journal on 12 August 2026

body: A common trick is a phone call that sounds like your son, your daughter or a close friend. The caller cries or sounds afraid. They say there was an accident, a hospital bill or a police case, and they need money at once. The voice may be a copy made by an AI tool from a recording of the real person. Today a voice is not proof of who is speaking. Do not send money only because the voice sounds right.

In a 'digital arrest' scam, someone calls and says they are from the police, the CBI, customs or TRAI. They say your Aadhaar, your SIM or a parcel is linked to a crime. Then they keep you on a video call for hours or even days. They show a fake office and uniform, and tell you to move your money to a 'safe' account. This is always a fraud. Indian law has no digital arrest. Real agencies do not question people or collect money on video calls.

Fake videos of well-known people are used to sell investment schemes. The video may show a famous business leader, a minister or a top banker promising high and fast profit. The face and voice look real, but a computer made them. In November 2024 the Reserve Bank of India warned that fake videos of its Governor were being shared online. It said the RBI does not give such investment advice. Government data shows that investment fraud took about three-fourths of all the money lost to cyber fraud in 2025.

Many scams start with a WhatsApp message or SMS. It may say your bank KYC has expired, a traffic challan is unpaid, or a quick loan is ready. The message carries a link or a file ending in .apk. If you install it, criminals can read your SMS and OTPs and take money from your bank or UPI app. In July 2026 the government's PIB Fact Check unit warned about fake e-challan links and APK files. By June 2026 the government had blocked 3,718 apps, including fake loan apps.

AI makes these old tricks harder to spot. Earlier, a fake message often had poor language, and a fake caller had a strange voice. Now AI tools can write clean messages in English, Hindi or other languages. They can copy a voice from a recording, and they can put a real person's face on a false video. So a call, message or video can look and sound correct and still be false. The warning signs have not changed: fear, hurry, secrecy, and a demand for money or an OTP.

A few simple habits will protect you. If a caller asks for money, cut the call and phone the person back on the number you have saved. Agree on a family code word that only your family knows, and ask for it in any emergency call. No real police officer, court or agency arrests anyone on a video call. Never share an OTP, UPI PIN or card number with anyone. You do not need an OTP or PIN to receive money. Install apps only from the official app store.

If you have lost money, act fast. Call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 at once, and tell your bank too. Then file a complaint on the official portal, cybercrime.gov.in. Quick reports help stop the money before criminals take it out. Keep screenshots, phone numbers and payment details as proof. If you only got a suspicious call, SMS or WhatsApp message and lost no money, report it on Chakshu. Chakshu is in the Sanchar Saathi app and at sancharsaathi.gov.in. Your report helps the telecom department act against that number.
tips: If a 'family member' calls for urgent money, hang up and call back on the number you have saved.
Choose a family code word and ask for it in any emergency call.
Cut any video call where 'police', 'CBI' or 'customs' says you are under arrest. Digital arrest does not exist in law.
Never share an OTP, UPI PIN, card number or bank password with anyone.
Do not install .apk files or open links sent on WhatsApp or SMS.
Do not trust a video of a famous person promising quick profit.
If money is lost, call 1930 at once and file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in.
Report suspicious calls and messages on Chakshu in the Sanchar Saathi app or at sancharsaathi.gov.in.

world.title: AI advice and quick tests helped 7,000 chilli farmers grow more
world.summary: About 7,000 chilli farmers in Khammam district got AI-based crop advice, quick soil tests and camera-based quality checks under the Saagu Baagu project. The World Economic Forum reported 21% more chilli per acre and lower pesticide use in the pilot.

stats.label: More chilli per acre in the pilot
stats.source: World Economic Forum team, article published by ThePrint, January 2024

stats.label: Extra income per acre in one crop cycle, as reported by the programme
stats.source: World Economic Forum team, January 2024; repeated in a NITI Aayog report, November 2025

stats.label: Chilli farmers in the first phase
stats.source: Telangana Government, reported by Telangana Today, July 2023

body: Khammam district in Telangana grows a lot of chilli. Many farmers there have small plots. They face pest attacks, high costs for fertiliser and pesticide, and prices that change every season. Good advice often reached them late. A normal soil test could take several weeks. Buyers judged chilli quality by eye, so a farmer could not easily prove that the crop deserved a better price.

The Telangana government started Saagu Baagu with the World Economic Forum. The non-profit Digital Green ran it with agritech start-ups, with support from the Gates Foundation. About 7,000 chilli farmers got four services: crop advice from a Telugu WhatsApp chatbot, a soil test that used machine learning and gave results in under an hour, a camera-based AI check of chilli quality, and an online platform to sell the crop.

The World Economic Forum team published the pilot results in January 2024. The pilot ran for 18 months and three crop cycles. The team said chilli yield per acre rose 21%, pesticide use fell 9%, fertiliser use fell 5% and the price per unit rose 8% because quality was better. It said income rose by more than ₹66,000 per acre in one crop cycle. A NITI Aayog report in November 2025 repeated these results.

These figures come from the programme partners. No independent study was found. The farmers got four services together, so nobody can say how much of the gain came from AI alone. Reports also differ: one gives the price gain as 8%, another as 11%. In October 2023 the State announced a larger phase for 5 lakh farmers in 10 districts. No published results for that larger phase were found.
tips: A soil test before you buy fertiliser can save money. Ask your local agriculture office where you can get one.
When a programme reports a big rise in income, ask who measured it and whether farmers outside the programme were compared.
Crop advice works best in your own language. Ask your agriculture officer which official WhatsApp or phone advice services cover your crop.

world.title: AI monsoon forecasts reached 3.88 crore farmers by SMS
world.summary: In Kharif 2025 the Agriculture Ministry sent AI-based forecasts of when steady rain would start to 3.88 crore farmers in 13 states. In Government follow-up surveys in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar, 31 to 52 percent of farmers said they changed their planting plans.

stats.label: Farmers who were sent the forecasts by SMS in Kharif 2025
stats.source: Government of India (PIB Research), February 2026

stats.label: Surveyed farmers in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar who changed planting decisions
stats.source: Government of India (PIB Research), February 2026, and a Lok Sabha reply, March 2026

stats.label: How early the forecast came before the rain
stats.source: Ministry of Agriculture, reported by Free Press Journal (IANS), September 2025

body: Most kharif crops depend on monsoon rain. If a farmer sows early and the rain then stops, the seed, diesel and labour can be lost. If the farmer waits too long, the season becomes short. Older forecasts told farmers when the monsoon would reach Kerala. They did not say when steady rain would reach the farmer's own area two to four weeks later.

In 2025 the Ministry of Agriculture worked with the India Meteorological Department and the Development Innovation Lab-India, which is linked to the University of Chicago. Researchers tested several weather models. They then mixed two open AI models, Google's NeuralGCM and the European AIFS, with 125 years of Indian rainfall records. Farmers got SMS messages through m-Kisan in Hindi, Odia, Marathi, Bangla and Punjabi.

The Government says the messages went to 3.88 crore farmers in 13 states, up to four weeks before the rain. In 2025 the monsoon came early and then paused for about 20 days. The Ministry said the forecast had warned of this pause. Feedback collected in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar found that 31 to 52 percent of farmers changed their plans, mainly land preparation, sowing dates and crop choice.

The feedback was collected by the Government through Kisan Call Centres, in two states only. The papers checked do not give the number of farmers surveyed. No study has yet shown that crops or income improved. A forecast gives a chance, not a promise, and an SMS helps only if it is read and understood. For Kharif 2026 the Government planned a national system, but no reach figures were found.
tips: A forecast gives a chance. A 70% chance of rain means it can still be wrong about 3 times in 10, so keep a backup plan.
The forecasts came by SMS through the Government's m-Kisan service. Ask your agriculture office how to register your mobile number for it.
Before you change your crop or sowing date, check the forecast with local advice from your agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra.

world.summary: In a 2022 study in and around Kolkata, 1,670 women were offered paid phone work that helps build AI for Bengali and Hindi. Far more women started the work when they could do it at home than when it was in an office.

body: In and around Kolkata, many married women have never worked for pay. In one study group of 1,670 women, the average age was about 30. Of these women, 93% were married and 69% had never had a paid job. Only 36% said the final decision to take a job was their own. Housework and child care make a fixed-hours office job hard to accept.

In 2022 researchers offered these women real paid work on a smartphone through Project Karya, which began at Microsoft Research in India. The work helps build AI for Indian languages. A woman records herself reading sentences in Bengali or Hindi and checks that recordings are labelled correctly. The women were placed by lottery into groups. Some were offered office work. Others were offered the same work at home, at fixed or free hours.

The researchers, whose summary is published by the J-PAL research network, found that only 14.6% of women offered the office job started work. Among women offered the most flexible home job, the share was 33 percentage points higher. Working at home while caring for children mattered more than free hours. Ten weeks later, women who had held a flexible job were 6 percentage points more likely to take up another job offer.

The study covered one area for two rounds of four weeks, so it does not show long-term earnings. Pay was small: about Re 1 per task, up to ₹4,000 in all. Women who moved from office work to home work produced 19% less per minute. The work ran on Karya's platform, so the study was not fully separate from Karya. This kind of work is extra income, not a full job.
tips: Honest task work pays you. Do not pay any joining fee to get phone-based 'AI task' or data work.
Phone work at home can be a first step into paid work, but treat it as extra income and keep any steady work you have.
Before you record your voice for anyone, ask who will use it, how much you will be paid and when.

world.title: Farmers ask an AI app by voice; women rate it higher than men
world.summary: Farmer.Chat, made by the non-profit Digital Green, answers farming questions by voice, text or photo in local languages. In surveys by outside research firms, most users said advice became easier to get and about 60% of active users said they acted on it.

stats.label: Women users in India who said their quality of life improved within 45 days (men: 55%)

body: A small farmer often has nobody to ask when a pest appears or frost is coming. Government extension workers cannot reach every farm in time. Women farmers get even less advice. Researchers at CGAP note that women are less likely than men to have a smartphone, have less money of their own for mobile data and may read less easily. Advice that comes late is of little use.

Digital Green, a non-profit, built Farmer.Chat in 2023. It is an Android app. A farmer asks a question by voice, by typing or by sending a photo, in a local language. The AI answers using research material and content checked by experts, and it considers the place, the crop and the weather. It was first given to more than 5,000 government extension workers in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand.

A December 2025 report in The Hans India gave more than 3.5 lakh farmers in India and over 30 lakh questions. Surveys by the research firm 60 Decibels found that 83% of users said information became much easier to get. In its 2024 India study, 61% of women and 55% of men said their quality of life improved within 45 days. An IDinsight assessment found about 60% of active users acted on the advice.

These surveys record what farmers say. They do not measure yield or income. Women are a large group of users but not the majority: reports give 35% in December 2025 and about 45% in March 2026. AI answers can be wrong. A technical paper from November 2025 says the safety methods reduce wrong answers but do not remove them, and that voice replies are still slow. A smartphone is needed.
tips: Farmer.Chat is an Android app, and reports say its basic advice will stay free. If typing is hard, ask your question by voice.
Treat an AI answer as a first opinion. Check any pesticide name and dose with the product label or your agriculture officer before you spray.
If one phone is shared at home, make sure the woman who does the farm work can also ask her own questions.

A helper that listens and replies in the farmer's own language can remove this difficulty.

A sick cow or buffalo cannot say what is wrong, and every day of lower milk means lower income. The producer needs quick, trusted advice on illness, feed, vaccination and breeding. He said many farmers, a large number of them women, were using it, but he gave no count.

As of 25 November 2026, no published count of Sarlaben's users or questions was found. No study shows better animal health or higher income. The share of women among actual users is not published. It started in one language, with more planned. One trade report noted that smartphone and data use differ from home to home. This is a large new service whose benefit is not yet measured.

world.summary: Punjab's health department used an AI tool that reads heat pictures to screen 15,069 women for breast cancer. The department's own published study says 27 cancers were confirmed after follow-up tests.

stats.label: Women screened at 183 government sites in 18 months
stats.source: Punjab Department of Health and Family Welfare, published in npj Digital Medicine, January 2025

stats.label: Women confirmed to have breast cancer after follow-up tests
stats.source: Punjab Department of Health and Family Welfare, published in npj Digital Medicine, January 2025

stats.label: High-risk women for whom no follow-up details were available
stats.source: Punjab Department of Health and Family Welfare, published in npj Digital Medicine, January 2025

body: Breast cancer is found late in many Indian women. A mammogram needs a costly machine and a trained doctor, and many small towns do not have them. Under the national programme, a health worker checks for lumps by hand. Many women never get any check at all. Punjab's health department wanted a test that could travel to small government hospitals and that women would accept.

From June 2022 to December 2023, Punjab ran screening in all 23 districts. The test, called Thermalytix, is made by the company Niramai. A camera takes heat pictures of the chest without touching the woman and without radiation. AI software reads the pictures and gives a risk level. ASHA workers and nurses brought women aged 30 and above. Women marked as high risk were sent for scans and guided by phone.

Officials of the department published the results in the journal npj Digital Medicine in January 2025. In 18 months, 15,069 women were screened at 183 sites. The software marked 460 women, about 3 in every 100, as high risk. Follow-up details were available for 268 of them. Doctors confirmed breast cancer in 27 women. Treatment had started for 18 of them when the study was written.

There are clear limits. No follow-up details were available for 192 of the 460 high-risk women; most of them did not share their reports. Women marked as low risk were not tested again, so the study cannot say how many cancers the tool missed. It did not compare the tool directly with a mammogram or a hand check. Niramai did the screening, and the authors work for the department that ran the programme.
tips: Women aged 30 and above can ask an ASHA worker or the nearest government health centre about breast screening under the government programme.
A screening result is not a diagnosis. If you are sent for a scan or biopsy, go, and keep your reports.
Any lump or change in the breast needs a doctor, whatever a screening test said.

world.title: AI helped a free call service keep more mothers listening
world.summary: ARMMAN's free mMitra voice calls give health advice to pregnant women and new mothers in Mumbai and nearby cities. Trials by Google and ARMMAN found that AI-chosen follow-up calls reduced drop-outs, with small gains in some health habits.

stats.label: Fewer drops in listening in the AI group, in a 7-week test with about 23,000 women
stats.source: Google Research, the AI team's own blog, 24 August 2022

stats.label: Women in the second trial, run in 2023 and 2024
stats.source: Authors from Google DeepMind, IIT Bombay and ARMMAN, arXiv preprint, 28 July 2025

stats.label: Higher chance of taking calcium tablets after delivery, from a phone survey
stats.source: Authors from Google DeepMind, IIT Bombay and ARMMAN, arXiv preprint, 28 July 2025

body: Many pregnant women in poor city areas get little health advice between clinic visits. The charity ARMMAN runs mMitra, a free service that started in 2013. It sends short recorded voice calls with advice timed to the week of pregnancy or the age of the baby. But many women stop answering after a few weeks. ARMMAN has only a small team that can phone women personally, so it must choose whom to call.

With researchers from Google, ARMMAN built an AI model. Each week it studies how long each woman listened to past calls. It then picks the women for whom a personal call from a health worker is likely to help most. The health worker, not the AI, speaks to the mother. Google's researchers work only with data that has names removed. The trial covered mothers in Mumbai, Palghar, Pune and Nashik.

In 2022, Google Research reported a seven-week test with about 23,000 women. The group helped by the AI had 32 per cent fewer drops in listening than the usual-care group. A second trial in 2023 and 2024 covered 34,453 women. In a phone survey afterwards, mothers who got an AI-chosen call were about 28 per cent more likely to be taking calcium tablets after delivery. They also scored better on a question about the baby's birth weight.

The limits are important. Both studies were written by Google and ARMMAN staff, not by outside researchers. The second study is a preprint, which means other experts have not yet reviewed it. Only about 1,500 women answered the survey. The gain in iron tablet use was too weak to rule out chance. Most other survey questions, such as breastfeeding and cord care, showed no clear change. These studies did not measure illness or deaths.
tips: mMitra and the Government's Kilkari health calls are free. Pregnant women can ask an ASHA worker or the government hospital whether they are registered.
A recorded call gives general advice only. For any worry in pregnancy, see a doctor or nurse.
Here the AI only chooses who gets a human call. It does not replace the health worker.

world.title: Delhi slum camps used AI on chest X-rays and found 877 TB cases
world.summary: Delhi's TB programme held chest X-ray camps in slum clusters and used Qure.ai software to pick people for a lab test. A study by the programme's own team reported 877 confirmed TB cases among 1,68,568 people screened.

stats.label: People given a chest X-ray at 3,566 camps, July 2025 to March 2026
stats.source: Delhi State TB programme and The Union, in the Indian Journal of Tuberculosis, August 2026, as reported by PTI on 6 October 2026

stats.label: People confirmed to have TB by a lab test
stats.source: Delhi State TB programme and The Union, in the Indian Journal of Tuberculosis, August 2026, as reported by PTI on 6 October 2026

stats.label: People marked by the AI who did not complete the lab test
stats.source: Same study, as reported by The Pioneer on 8 October 2026

body: TB spreads through the air and is common in crowded homes. Many people with TB have no cough or fever at first, so asking about symptoms misses them. India's national TB survey found that over 40 per cent of confirmed cases reported none of the usual symptoms. A chest X-ray can show early signs, but slum areas have few X-ray machines and very few doctors to read the pictures.

From July 2025 to March 2026, Delhi's TB programme and the health group The Union held 3,566 camps in 349 slum clusters across six districts. Camps ran in anganwadi centres, schools and community halls. Anyone aged 15 or above could get a chest X-ray on a small handheld machine. Software from the company Qure.ai marked X-rays that looked like TB. Those people were asked to give a sputum sample for a lab test.

The team published its results in the Indian Journal of Tuberculosis in August 2026, and the news agency PTI reported them in October. Of 1,68,568 people X-rayed, the software marked 18,377, about 11 in every 100. Of these, 16,866 completed the lab test, and 877 had confirmed TB. That is one confirmed case for every 192 people screened. The lab test, not the AI, made the final diagnosis.

The study was written by the same agencies that ran the camps, so it is not an outside check. About 8 in every 100 marked people did not complete the lab test. News reports of the study do not say how many TB cases the software missed, or how many patients finished treatment. A marked X-ray is not a diagnosis: about 95 of every 100 people who were marked and tested did not have TB.
tips: TB tests and treatment are free at government health centres. The national TB helpline is 1800-11-6666.
If a screening camp asks you to give a sputum sample, give it. Only the lab test can confirm TB.
A person can have TB without a cough. Ask about screening if someone in your home has TB.

world.title: Andhra students using adaptive maths software learned faster
world.summary: Andhra Pradesh government schools give Class 6 to 9 students tablet lessons that adjust to each child's level. University of Chicago researchers said in September 2025 that these students gained nearly two extra years of maths learning in about 17 months.

stats.label: Extra learning in about 17 months, compared with schools without the software
stats.source: Development Innovation Lab, University of Chicago, announced on 8 September 2025

stats.label: Schools that got the software and schools that did not, chosen by lottery
stats.source: AEA RCT Registry, entry filed by the research team, updated March 2026

stats.label: In each school's lab, used in 2 of the 8 weekly maths periods
stats.source: AEA RCT Registry, entry filed by the research team, updated March 2026

body: In many government schools, children in one class are at very different levels in maths. Some children are far behind the level of their textbook. One teacher with a full classroom cannot teach each child at the right level, and children who fall behind often stay behind. Andhra Pradesh wanted a way to give each child practice that starts from what that child already knows.

The state began its Personalised Adaptive Learning programme, called PAL, in 2019 in about 520 schools. Each school got a lab with 30 tablets. Students in Classes 6 to 9 use them in two of their eight weekly maths periods. The software first tests the child on a chapter. It then picks videos and questions to fit that child. Software like this is often counted as a simple form of AI: it adapts, but it does not chat.

Researchers from the Development Innovation Lab at the University of Chicago, led by Nobel Prize winner Michael Kremer, studied PAL. The trial registry says schools were chosen by lottery: 60 got PAL and 60 did not. In September 2025, the team said PAL students gained nearly two extra years of learning over about 17 months, more than double the usual rate. They announced this at a public event in Delhi.

Some things are still not known. The result was shared at an event organised by Central Square Foundation and ConveGenius.AI, an education technology company. In November 2026, the trial registry showed no posted results, and the trial runs until 2027. The study measured maths only. A summary of a report in The Hindu says that running PAL across the whole state needs a large budget and many more tablets.
tips: Parents in Andhra Pradesh can ask the school if it has a PAL lab and how many periods a week the children use it.
In this programme, children use the software inside school hours with a teacher present, not alone at home.
Ask who measured a learning app's results. A lottery-based study by outside researchers is stronger than a company's own claim.

world.title: Karnataka teachers saved two hours a week with an AI planner
world.summary: More than 1,000 Karnataka government school teachers used Shiksha Copilot, an AI tool that drafts lesson plans from state textbooks. A Cornell University and Microsoft Research study found that teachers reported saving about two hours a week.

stats.label: Teachers in 757 schools who used the tool, December 2024 to March 2025
stats.source: Cornell University and Microsoft Research India study, arXiv, version of March 2026

stats.label: Less time spent on lesson planning each week, as reported by 406 teachers
stats.source: Cornell University and Microsoft Research India study, arXiv, version of March 2026

stats.label: Parts of Kannada lesson plans that human reviewers had to edit
stats.source: Same study, as reported by the Cornell Chronicle on 8 October 2026

body: Government school teachers must prepare a lesson plan for every class, and often have to submit it on paper. This takes hours each week, on top of teaching, records and other duties. Lesson material made elsewhere may use examples that village children do not know, and may not match the state textbook. Teachers in Karnataka told researchers that this paperwork left them less time and energy for teaching.

Microsoft Research India built Shiksha Copilot with the Bengaluru non-profit Sikshana Foundation. The tool reads Karnataka's textbooks and drafts lesson plans in English with a large AI model. Another model translates them into Kannada. It uses local examples, such as dosa in place of pizza. Trained reviewers check the ready-made plans before teachers use them. From December 2024 to March 2025, 1,043 teachers in 757 schools used it.

Researchers from Cornell University and Microsoft Research India studied this period. In surveys before and after, 406 teachers reported spending about two hours less each week on lesson planning. Their stress scores fell a little. Teachers rated about 85 in every 100 plans as very good. Some said they now used more activities and fewer lectures. The study received an honourable mention at the ACM CSCW conference in October 2026.

The AI made many language errors in Kannada. Reviewers had to edit more than 9 in every 10 parts of the Kannada plans, against about 4 in 100 for English. The time saved is what teachers reported, not a measured figure. The study did not test whether students learned more. It covered about four months in one state. Microsoft staff, whose team built the tool, were among the authors.
tips: AI writing in Indian languages still needs a careful human check before it is used.
Teachers can treat an AI lesson plan as a first draft and change it for their own class.
Ask whether a school AI tool was tested for student learning, not only for time saved.

world.title: Ninety blind users tested AI glasses; reading worked best
world.summary: Ninety blind and low-vision people at five eye care centres used Indian-made Smart Vision Glasses for one month. A 2025 study in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology found that most liked the reading feature, but few found the walking help useful.

stats.label: Blind and low-vision users at five centres, one month each, in 2022
stats.source: Authors from Vision-Aid, SHG Technologies and universities, Indian Journal of Ophthalmology, June 2025

stats.label: Users who found the reading feature useful
stats.source: Authors from Vision-Aid, SHG Technologies and universities, Indian Journal of Ophthalmology, June 2025

stats.label: Users who found the walking help useful
stats.source: Authors from Vision-Aid, SHG Technologies and universities, Indian Journal of Ophthalmology, June 2025

body: A blind person often needs someone else to read a letter, a medicine label or a page of a book. The study says India has about 48 lakh blind people and about 47 lakh more with severe vision loss. Blind students in particular need a way to read printed books and notes on their own. The makers wanted a low-cost device that also reads Indian languages.

Smart Vision Glasses are made by SHG Technologies of Bengaluru with the non-profit Vision-Aid. A small camera unit fits on a spectacle frame and works with an Android phone. AI software describes things nearby, reads printed text aloud, warns of obstacles and recognises saved faces. It reads English and nine Indian languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Marathi. In 2022, 90 people at five centres in Madurai, Chennai, Delhi and Pune borrowed a device for one month.

The results were published in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology in June 2025. All users could operate every feature. About 73 in 100 found the reading feature useful. Fewer found the other features useful: 45 in 100 for describing things nearby, 37 for face recognition and 22 for walking help. About 6 in 10 used the device for an hour or more each day. Most users were young, and nearly two-thirds were students.

Two authors work for Vision-Aid and one works for the maker, so this is not an outside test. The study recorded what users said, not how well they did tasks. All of them already used smartphones. Outdoor use was not tested. Users complained about battery life and the need for internet. The paper gives a price of 360 US dollars, and the phone is extra. Walking help was the feature users most wanted improved.
tips: Ask the low vision centre at an eye hospital whether you can try a device before buying it.
Some hospitals give AI glasses free through charity programmes, so ask before paying.
Do not depend on AI glasses alone when walking on roads. Keep using a cane or a guide.

world.title: Central complaint portal adds AI sorting and a voice helper
world.summary: CPGRAMS, the Central Government's complaint portal, uses AI to sort complaints and, since May 2026, a voice chatbot called Samadhan Didi. The Government reports that a complaint now takes 14 days on average to close.

stats.label: Average time for Central ministries to close a complaint in 2026 (157 days in 2014)
stats.source: Government of India, PIB Research Unit, 9 August 2026

stats.label: Citizen satisfaction rate, January to June 2026
stats.source: Government of India, PIB Research Unit, 9 August 2026

stats.label: Indian languages the Samadhan Didi voice chatbot supported at launch
stats.source: News On AIR (Government broadcaster), 30 May 2026

body: Many people have a complaint about a government service: a pension that has stopped, a subsidy that did not come, a road that is unsafe. Filing the complaint was hard. You had to know which ministry and which category to choose, and you had to type it. The Government says that in 2014 a complaint to a Central ministry took 157 days on average to close.

The Central Government runs one complaint portal for all ministries and States, called CPGRAMS, at pgportal.gov.in. It sends each complaint to the right officer automatically and uses AI to find common problems. On 30 May 2026 it added Samadhan Didi, a voice chatbot built with the Government's Bhashini language tools. A citizen speaks in one of 22 Indian languages. The chatbot asks a few questions, picks the ministry and category, and files the complaint.

The results here are the Government's own figures, published by its PIB Research Unit on 9 August 2026. Central ministries took 14 days on average to close a complaint in 2026. The portal closed 1,99,968 complaints in June 2026, and it has closed more than 1 lakh every month for 46 months. From January to June 2026 the citizen satisfaction rate was 76 percent.

No independent study of these figures was found. A satisfaction rate of 76 percent means about one in four people were not satisfied. A closed complaint is not always a solved problem. In 2021 a committee of Parliament found that some ministries closed complaints without giving reasons. The Government now plans to use AI to catch such cases. There are no published figures yet on how many people use Samadhan Didi, or how often it picks the wrong department.
tips: You can file a complaint about a government service free at pgportal.gov.in, in English or an Indian language.
Keep your registration number. If the reply does not solve your problem, rate it 'Poor' and file an appeal.
The portal does not take RTI requests, court matters or religious matters.

world.title: Maha Kumbh chatbot guided pilgrims in 11 languages
world.summary: At the Maha Kumbh 2025 in Prayagraj, a chatbot called Kumbh Sah'AI'yak used the Government's Bhashini language tools to answer pilgrims in 11 languages. Its builder reports that more than 3 lakh pilgrims used it.

stats.label: Languages the chatbot worked in: Hindi, English and nine others

body: The Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj ran from 13 January to 26 February 2025. Pilgrims came from every part of India and spoke many languages. For a visitor who did not know Hindi, simple things were hard: asking about a route, a place to stay or the bathing dates, or reporting a family member lost in the crowd.

The organisers offered a chatbot called Kumbh Sah'AI'yak on WhatsApp and on the Mela website and app. A pilgrim could type or speak a question and get the answer as text or voice. Answers came from a prepared set of facts about the Mela. Bhashini, the Government's language platform, did the translation and speech work. A firm called Samagra built the chatbot with the Mela authority and the Uttar Pradesh IT agency.

The Government's PIB Research Unit confirmed in February 2026 that the chatbot worked in 11 languages. Samagra, the builder, reported in March 2025 that more than 3 lakh pilgrims used it before and during the Mela. Questions about travel and stay were the most common. English and Hindi were used most, followed by Gujarati. The Government also says Bhashini has handled more than 400 crore language tasks across all its services.

Three lakh users is a very small share of the more than 65 crore visitors that Samagra cites for the Mela. The user figure comes from the builder and has not been checked by anyone independent. No figure has been published for how many answers were correct. Samagra itself reported problems: the speech tool misheard some accents and dialects, strict safety rules sometimes gave incomplete answers, and a phone-number login kept some users away.
tips: When a government app or website has a language menu or a mic button, try it in your own language.
Speak slowly and clearly. Speech tools still make mistakes with local accents and place names.
For anything important, such as a route, a date or a fee, confirm the chatbot's answer at an official help desk.

world.title: Kerala trial courts record witness statements with AI typing
world.summary: Since 1 November 2025, the Kerala High Court has told all trial courts in the State to record witness statements with Adalat AI, a speech-to-text tool. The order followed a test in four Ernakulam courts, but measured results for Kerala are not yet published.

stats.label: Ernakulam trial courts in the test from 1 February 2025, before the order for the whole State
stats.source: Kerala High Court office memorandum of 27 September 2025, reported by Bar and Bench, 3 October 2025

stats.label: Courts in nine states reported to have moved to AI typing
stats.source: ThePrint ground report, 27 October 2025

stats.label: Judges reached in 11 partner states, as the company claims

body: In a trial court, every word a witness says must be written down. In Kerala the judge wrote it by hand, or dictated it in open court, or a court typist typed it. This is slow work, and a judge can hear only a few witnesses in a day. Slow recording is one reason why cases take years. ThePrint reported that India has about 5 crore pending cases.

Kerala tested a speech-to-text tool called Adalat AI in four trial courts in Ernakulam district from 1 February 2025. The tool listens in court and shows the spoken words as text on a screen. The judge must check the text before it is signed and becomes part of the record. By an office memorandum dated 27 September 2025, the Kerala High Court told all courts in the State to use the tool for witness statements from 1 November 2025.

The legal news sites Bar and Bench and LiveLaw reported the High Court order in October 2025. ThePrint reported in the same month that more than 4,000 courts in nine states had moved to AI typing. One district judge in Patna told ThePrint that eight cases now got finished in a day in place of four. In November 2026 the company's website claimed 11 partner states and more than 6,000 judges reached.

No measured results for Kerala have been published. There are no public figures for time saved or for mistakes, and the company's claims have not been checked by anyone independent. ThePrint reported that early Kerala trials in Malayalam had many errors, and that the company then released a new Malayalam version. A researcher at DAKSH, a civil society group, warned that one misheard name can change a record. Kerala's own court guidelines say AI tools can be wrong.
tips: If you give evidence in court, ask to read your statement before you sign it. Check names, dates and amounts.
In these courts the AI only types what is spoken. The judge still decides the case.
Supreme Court judgments translated into Indian languages can be read free on the eSCR portal.

world.title: Villagers earn by recording their own languages for AI
world.summary: Karya, a Bengaluru organisation, pays people in villages and small towns to record and check speech in Indian languages, which is used to train AI. Karya reports that it had paid 4.42 million US dollars in wages by July 2026.

stats.label: Wages paid directly to workers so far

body: AI tools such as voice assistants and chatbots learn from examples. For most Indian languages there are few recorded examples, so these tools work poorly in them. At the same time, many people in villages, most of all women, have a phone but no paid work near home. Karya says 72 percent of its workers had no income of their own before they joined.

Karya began in 2017 as a Microsoft Research project in Bengaluru and became a separate organisation in 2021. It breaks big language jobs into small tasks on a phone app. A worker reads sentences aloud in her own language, or listens and writes down what others said. Companies and researchers buy this data to train AI. Karya finds workers through more than 200 local non-profit groups. Microsoft reported in 2024 that it paid about 5 US dollars an hour.

Karya's own figures, dated July 2026, say it has paid 4.42 million US dollars in wages. It says more than 2 lakh workers in 28 states have signed up, and that it has built data in more than 115 languages. From workers' survey answers, it reports an average rise of 25.8 percent in yearly income in 2025-26, and 35 percent for women.

These numbers come from Karya and have not been independently audited. The income gains rest on what workers said in surveys. This is task work, not a steady job. Microsoft described one woman in Pune who earned ₹2,000 for about five hours of work spread over 11 days. Total wages divided by all signed-up workers come to only about 22 US dollars each, so many workers have earned little. The work depends on orders from technology companies.
tips: Honest data work pays you. Never pay a fee to get a data-entry or AI task job.
Small phone tasks can add to your income, but they are not a full-time job. Do not leave steady work for them.
Before you record your voice for anyone, ask who will use it and how you will be paid.

body: An ASHA is a woman from the village who is its first health contact. She visits homes and advises on pregnancy, vaccines, child care and family planning. She gets only about 23 days of basic training. When a family asks a hard question, she may not know the answer. She may also feel shy to ask her supervisor, most of all on private subjects such as contraception.

Khushi Baby, a non-profit, built ASHABot with technology from Microsoft Research. It works inside WhatsApp, which the workers already use. An ASHA types or speaks her question in Hindi. The chatbot answers from about 40 documents from the Government, UNICEF and other health bodies. If it does not find a clear answer, it does not guess. It sends the question to a small group of nurses and passes their agreed answer back, usually within hours.

A research paper presented at the CHI computing conference in 2025 studied 20 ASHAs in Salumbar, Rajasthan, for 107 days in 2024. They sent 1,761 messages. The chatbot answered 1,348 health questions by itself and sent 264 to nurses. In tests before launch, doctors judged at least 85 percent of answers correct. Microsoft reported in June 2025 that 869 ASHAs had joined and had sent more than 24,000 messages.

This is still small. Microsoft said the chatbot was used in only one district of Rajasthan, while India has about ten lakh ASHAs. The study was short and based on interviews, and it reported no effect on patients' health. Nurses said yes to only about one in five requests for help, and worried about extra work. Some ASHAs trusted the chatbot too much.
tips: A careful health chatbot says 'I do not know' and asks a trained person. Be careful with tools that always have an answer.
Use a chatbot to check facts, then confirm serious health matters with a nurse or doctor.
If typing is hard for you, look for tools that take voice messages in your language.

world.title: AI in India's farming and food
world.summary: Indian farmers can now get crop, weather and scheme advice from AI helplines and chatbots. The reach is large, but proof that it raises farm incomes is still thin.

body: AI is already reaching Indian farms, mostly through the phone. Kisan e-Mitra, a Government voice chatbot launched in 2023, answers questions on schemes such as PM-KISAN, Kisan Credit Card and crop insurance. By December 2025 it had answered more than 93 lakh queries in 11 regional languages. In February 2026 the Agriculture Ministry launched Bharat-VISTAAR, an AI advisory service. Farmers can call the helpline 155261 and speak to it, so a smartphone is not needed.

AI is also used for weather and pests. In Kharif 2025, an AI-based pilot sent local monsoon onset forecasts by SMS to about 3.88 crore farmers in 13 states. In follow-up surveys in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar, 31 to 52 percent of farmers said they changed sowing or land preparation plans. The National Pest Surveillance System lets a farmer or field worker upload a photo of a damaged crop. It covers 66 crops and more than 432 pests.

Crop insurance and markets are changing too. Under the PMFBY crop insurance scheme, a system called YES-TECH uses satellite data and AI to estimate yields, and CROPIC uses dated, location-tagged crop photos to check damage. The aim is faster and fairer claims. The Government is also building AgriStack, a digital Farmer ID linked to land records. More than 7.63 crore IDs had been made by late November 2025. Bharat-VISTAAR brings weather, mandi prices, pest alerts and scheme information into one place.

What does this mean for people who farm? So far, AI in Indian farming gives advice. It does not do the field work, and there is no clear evidence that it is replacing farm jobs. Over 10,000 extension workers use the pest system as a tool in their own work. What is not yet known is important. No independent study shows that these services have raised farm incomes across India, and little public data shows how many farmers really use Bharat-VISTAAR.

States and private firms are active too. Maharashtra's MahaVistaar and Gujarat's AmulAI work as state-level services linked to the national platform. A Government note describes a Tamil Nadu startup, Farm Again, whose soil sensors have been used by over 3,500 farmers to manage water and fertiliser. But gaps remain. Bharat-VISTAAR started in Hindi and English only, and a policy review in October 2026 found that wider language coverage still depended on the state platforms.

There are real risks. Advice from a machine can be wrong for your soil, water or local market. If many farmers get the same crop advice, too much of one crop can push prices down. A wrong forecast in extreme weather can cause loss, and it is not clear who is responsible. Farmers also share land and personal data, and the rules on who can see it are not fully clear. People with low digital skills, or no phone signal, may be left out.
tips: Treat AI advice as one opinion. Check it with your local agriculture officer or an experienced farmer nearby.
To try the Government service, call the Bharat-VISTAAR helpline 155261. A basic phone is enough.
A forecast gives a chance, not a promise. Keep a back-up plan before you sow.
Never share an OTP, bank PIN or password with any caller or chatbot that claims to be from a scheme.
For a crop insurance claim, keep your own dated photos and papers as well as the app record.
If a service does not work in your language, ask your state agriculture office which app does.

world.title: AI in India's health care
world.summary: AI now helps Indian health workers screen for TB and eye disease and supports tele-consultations. Doctors warn people not to use chatbots to diagnose or treat themselves.

stats.source: News On AIR (Akashvani), October 2026

body: AI is already used in India's public health system. eSanjeevani, the Government's telemedicine service, has crossed 50 crore consultations. It includes an AI tool that suggests possible diagnoses to the doctor or health worker during the consultation. In the TB programme, AI reads chest X-rays, and a phone app called Cough Against TB studies a recorded cough. Its developer, Wadhwani AI, says about 2.9 lakh people in 17 states had been screened with the app by June 2026.

AI also helps where specialists are few. MadhuNetrAI lets trained non-specialists take photos of the retina of people with diabetes, and the AI sorts who needs an eye doctor first. The Government says about 7,100 patients in 38 facilities have benefited. Another tool predicts which TB patients may do badly in treatment, so staff can follow up early. The Government reports a 27 percent fall in poor outcomes after it was deployed. These are official figures, not independent trials.

The Government has set out guidance. ICMR issued ethical guidelines for AI in health care in 2023. They cover developers, researchers, doctors and ethics committees, with sections on consent and governance. In February 2026 the Health Ministry released SAHI, a national strategy for AI in health care. It gives recommendations and is not a law. The Ministry also launched BODH, a platform built by IIT Kanpur and the National Health Authority to test health AI tools before wide use.

Health insurance is changing more quietly. The Government says AI is used to spot suspicious claims in the Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY scheme. For private insurance, the regulator IRDAI set up a seven-member working group on AI in June 2026. It was asked to study uses such as claims processing and fraud detection, and to suggest a framework within three months. When the group was announced there were no binding AI rules for insurers, so practices can differ between companies.

For doctors, nurses and frontline health workers, AI is so far a helper, not a replacement. The tools above are built to support staff and to send hard cases to specialists. The head of the National Medical Commission has said AI should not replace doctors, and a free AI awareness course for trainee doctors began in December 2025. What is not yet known is how AI is changing health jobs, workloads or pay. There is no India-wide data on this.

The biggest risk for ordinary people is self-treatment. In a 2026 BCG survey of internet users, 85 percent of Indian respondents said they use AI tools for health. In January 2026 an AIIMS doctor described a patient who took painkillers after asking a chatbot and suffered bleeding. Screening tools can also miss disease or raise false alarms, so a confirming test is needed. AI may work less well for groups missing from its training data. Health data privacy is another concern.
tips: Use a chatbot to understand medical words or prepare questions for your doctor. Do not use it to diagnose yourself or to start or stop a medicine.
In an emergency, go to a hospital or call 112. Do not wait for an app's answer.
If an AI screening test flags a problem, ask for the confirming test. A screening result is not a final diagnosis.
You can ask a hospital or clinic whether AI is used in your care and who checks its results.
If an insurance claim is refused, ask the insurer for the reason in writing and use its grievance process.
Before you upload reports or scans to an app, check who runs it and how your data is kept.

world.title: AI in India's schools, colleges and coaching
world.summary: AI is now in the CBSE curriculum from Class 3 and on many students' phones. Rules for using it in colleges are still unclear, and good learning still needs effort and teachers.

stats.source: Central Square Foundation BaSE 2025 survey, reported by PTI / ThePrint, February 2026

body: AI has entered Indian classrooms in two ways: as a subject and as a tool. On 1 April 2026 the Education Minister launched CBSE's new Computational Thinking and AI curriculum for Classes 3 to 8, for the 2026-27 school year. NCERT approved it, and there are handbooks for teachers. CBSE already offered a 15-hour AI skill module from Class 6 and AI as an optional subject in Classes 9 to 12. NCERT is also preparing AI textbooks for Classes 9 to 12.

Official platforms use AI too. DIKSHA, the Education Ministry's learning app, uses AI for keyword search inside videos and a read-aloud feature for visually impaired students. SWAYAM offers more than 110 free AI courses from IITs and IISc, with over 41.2 lakh enrolments. The SOAR programme gives AI lessons for Classes 6 to 12 and a 45-hour module for teachers. In February 2026 the Minister also launched Bodhan AI, a centre at IIT Madras for AI in education.

Students are not waiting for policy. A 2025 survey of 12,500 children in low-income homes across 10 states found that 96 percent of those who use generative AI use it for school learning. Most first heard of it from friends. Coaching firms are moving fast. PhysicsWallah says its AI tools now answer about 90 percent of student doubts, with a human expert stepping in when a student is not satisfied. These are company claims and have not been independently checked.

Exams are changing as well. The National Testing Agency said it would use facial recognition to check candidates in major entrance tests such as JEE and NEET from 2026. In August 2026 the Centre told the Supreme Court that the NEET paper is translated into 13 languages using AI. In colleges, rules are behind actual use. A Careers360 report in April 2026 found universities still waiting for UGC guidance, with some teachers adding oral questions to check written work.

For teachers, AI is changing the work, not removing it so far. CBSE made computational thinking and AI its teacher training theme for 2026-27, and News On AIR reported that teachers would be trained during the summer break. A coaching firm's co-founder has said he does not expect teachers to be replaced. What is not yet known is whether AI improves learning results in India, or how it will affect teaching and coaching jobs. There is no clear India-wide evidence yet.

The risks are real. AI can give wrong answers with full confidence, and a student who copies them learns little. In the same survey, 66 percent of parents and teachers who knew about generative AI said it adds to the risks of learning apps, mainly overuse and wrong information. Students told Careers360 that tools claiming to detect AI writing are often unreliable. Face checks in exams mean sharing face data. Children without phones or internet can fall further behind.
tips: Try the question yourself first. Then ask AI to explain your mistake, not to write the answer.
Check AI answers against your textbook or ask your teacher. AI can be wrong.
Ask your school or college what its rule on AI use is, and say when you have used it.
Parents: sit with younger children when they use AI apps, and agree time limits.
Look at free official courses on SWAYAM or DIKSHA before paying for an AI course.
For entrance exams, follow only official NTA notices on identity checks, not forwarded messages.

world.title: AI in India's banking, UPI and insurance
world.summary: Banks and payment apps in India use AI to catch fraud, answer customers and help decide loans. RBI wants humans to stay in charge, and fraudsters are using AI too.

stats.label: Share of 612 RBI-supervised banks and firms using or building AI systems
stats.source: Reserve Bank of India, FREE-AI Committee Report, August 2025

stats.label: Money Indians lost to cyber fraud in 2025, at least
stats.source: Ministry of Home Affairs data, reported by ThePrint, February 2026

stats.label: UPI transactions in October 2026 (25.47 billion)
stats.source: NPCI data, reported by Free Press Journal, November 2026

body: AI already works behind many money services in India. An RBI committee surveyed 612 banks and other supervised firms and found that 20.8 percent were using or building AI systems. The most common uses were customer support, credit underwriting, sales and cybersecurity. UPI, which handled about 2,547 crore transactions in October 2026, now has an AI helper too. MyUPI in the BHIM app lets users check payments, raise complaints and manage Autopay mandates in five languages.

Fraud is the biggest problem. Home Ministry data show Indians lost at least ₹22,495 crore to cyber fraud in 2025, across about 28 lakh reported cases. Investment scams made up about three-quarters of the money lost. RBI's Innovation Hub built MuleHunter.AI to find 'mule' accounts that criminals use to move stolen money. In May 2026 the Financial Services Secretary urged banks to adopt it quickly. No public figures show how many banks use it or how many accounts it has caught.

RBI has set out its thinking. Its FREE-AI report of August 2025 gives seven guiding principles and 26 recommendations. It says customers should be told when they are dealing with AI, and that AI credit decisions should be open to audit and human oversight. In June 2026 RBI issued draft guidance on managing the risks of models, including AI. ThePrint reported that the draft asks lenders to explain decisions, keep a way to switch a model off, and let customers reach a human.

Selling practices are also being regulated. New RBI directions for commercial banks, in force from 1 January 2027, stop banks from forcing an extra product on you with a loan or account. They require clear consent with 'No' as the default choice, and bar app designs that trick you into agreeing. If mis-selling is proved, the bank must refund the full amount. For insurance, IRDAI formed a working group on AI in June 2026. When it was announced, binding AI rules for insurers did not yet exist.

Jobs in banking are shifting. Business Today reported in July 2026 that HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Axis Bank all ended 2025-26 with fewer staff. At HDFC Bank, junior non-supervisory staff fell by over 8,000 while management roles grew. HDFC and Axis said they were not laying people off, but were not refilling some posts as technology raised output. Axis said this came more from general technology than from AI. How much AI itself is reducing bank jobs in India is not yet known.

There are risks for customers. An AI credit model can be unfair to people with little data history, and RBI's committee warned that bias could shut out people who are already excluded. Chatbots can misunderstand a problem or give a wrong answer. RBI's draft guidance is not final yet. Fraudsters use AI as well: SBI warned customers in January 2026 about fake videos and cloned voices of relatives or bank staff asking for urgent money. No tool catches every fraud.
tips: Treat any urgent request for money as suspicious, even if the voice or face is familiar. Call back on a number you already know.
Never share your OTP, UPI PIN, card CVV or passwords. No bank or AI assistant needs them.
If you are cheated, call the cybercrime helpline 1930 at once and tell your bank.
If a chatbot cannot solve your problem, ask for a human officer and note your complaint number.
If a loan or insurance claim is refused, ask for the reasons in writing.
Read before you tap 'I agree'. Say no to insurance or other add-ons you did not ask for.

world.title: AI for India's shops, MSMEs and online sellers
world.summary: Small Indian businesses are starting to use AI for customer chats, online selling and marketing. The tools are easy to try, but real gains are not yet proven.

body: AI is reaching small businesses mainly through tools they already use. In May 2026 Meta launched Business AI inside the WhatsApp Business app in India. It can answer customer questions at any hour, suggest products from the shop's catalogue, note leads and book appointments, in Indian languages. The owner can take over a chat or switch the AI off. Meta said UPI payment inside these chats would come later. The results it quotes are from individual businesses, not independent studies.

Government-backed networks are growing too. ONDC, the open network for online selling started by the Government's DPIIT, crossed 50 crore total transactions in July 2026. Its DigiDukaan service had linked over 21,000 kirana shops with more than 450 brands in Hyderabad, Jaipur and Mumbai by September 2026. On GeM, the Government's buying portal, micro and small enterprises completed orders worth over ₹2.36 lakh crore in 2025-26. The Commerce Minister has asked GeM to use AI more for price checks.

How many small firms really use AI? Surveys differ. A 2026 PayNearby survey of 10,000 retailers and small firms, many in small towns and villages, found 71 percent had used an AI tool in some way. But 26 percent were unsure which features would help them. A Vi Business study found that 25 percent of small firms had built AI into their operations. Both studies come from companies that sell services to small firms, so read them with care.

Support from the Government is mostly general so far. The IndiaAI Mission has an approved outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore for computing power, skills and startups. The Minister of State for MSME told the Lok Sabha in July 2026 that it also aims to help MSMEs. The MSME Ministry has trained over 2,500 PM Vishwakarma artisans to use AI tools for branding, design and marketing. The MSME TEAM programme aims to bring 5 lakh small enterprises onto ONDC.

For owners and workers, AI today mostly saves time on small tasks: replying to customers, writing about a product, or designing a label. It does not replace knowing your customers, your stock and your suppliers. ONDC's chief has said DigiDukaan is meant to strengthen local distributors, not replace them. What is not yet known is whether AI raises sales or profit for most small Indian firms, or whether it will reduce jobs for shop helpers and office staff.

There are risks to watch. An AI chat reply can quote a wrong price or promise something you cannot deliver, and you remain responsible to the customer. Customer data put into an AI tool may be stored by the company that runs it. Costs can change: NPCI has planned a fee on some UPI payments above ₹2,000 to merchants and has postponed its start. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh a month by UPI QR are exempt.
tips: Start small. Try AI on one task, such as replies to common customer questions, and check every answer at first.
Keep your catalogue, prices and timings up to date. An AI assistant can only repeat what you give it.
Do not paste customer phone numbers, Aadhaar numbers or bank details into public AI tools.
Confirm the money in your bank or UPI app before handing over goods. Do not rely on a screenshot.
Look at seller registration on ONDC and GeM to reach new buyers, and ask about help under the TEAM programme.
Ask your bank or payment app what charges apply to you before any new UPI fee starts.

world.summary: India's IT industry is still adding jobs, but much more slowly than its revenue grows. Freshers and call-centre workers feel the change most.

body: India's technology industry earned an estimated 315 billion US dollars in the financial year 2025-26, up 6.1%, says the industry body Nasscom. Work on AI brought in about 10 to 12 billion dollars of that. Nasscom says AI moved from trials to regular use in specific business tasks during the year, and that over 20 lakh tech workers have now had some AI training. Its chairperson said AI is changing the nature of work while also opening new opportunities.

Jobs are still growing, but slowly. Nasscom says the industry added about 1.35 lakh jobs in 2025-26 and employs about 59.5 lakh people. That is 2.3% more jobs against 6.1% more revenue. The five largest IT firms show a harder picture. TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra together ended 2025-26 with 7,389 fewer staff, after adding 12,718 the year before. From July to September 2026 they added 13,918 people between them, though Wipro's headcount fell by 6,716.

Is AI the cause? That is not proven. In July 2025 TCS said it would let go of about 12,000 people, around 2% of its staff, mostly middle and senior. Its chief executive said the reason was skills that no longer fitted the work, not AI doing people's jobs. The Economic Survey of January 2026 said large job losses from AI had not appeared so far, but urged caution. Asked in Parliament in December 2025 about studying such losses, the Labour Ministry listed training schemes but cited no study.

Freshers feel the change most. The staffing firm Xpheno estimates that Indian IT hired about 6 lakh freshers in 2021-22 but only about 1.2 lakh in 2024-25. Companies point to weak demand and cost pressure as well as AI. Hiring continues but is more selective. TCS took in about 24,000 graduates in the first half of 2026-27, and Infosys kept its target of 20,000 for the year. The IT ministry told Parliament in July 2026 that junior testing and basic support roles are the most exposed to automation.

Call centres and back-office work face a sharp test. Reuters reported in October 2025 that this part of the industry employs about 16.5 lakh people, and that it added fewer than 17,000 jobs in each of the past two years, against 1.3 lakh in 2022-23. Indian firms such as LimeChat say their chatbots let clients answer the same number of customer queries with far fewer staff. These are company claims. A NITI Aayog report warned that customer-service jobs could fall to about 18 lakh by 2031.

Much remains uncertain. NITI Aayog said 15 to 20 lakh tech jobs could go within five years if nothing is done, and up to 40 lakh new ones could be created with a national plan. Both are forecasts, not facts. Training has gaps too: the Government's FutureSkills PRIME portal had 18.56 lakh sign-ups by December 2025, but only 3.37 lakh people had finished a course. The IT workers' union NITES says hiring targets announced by companies do not always turn into real jobs.
tips: If your work is testing, basic support or routine coding, start learning now how to check and guide AI tools.
Finish any AI course you start, such as those on the Government-backed FutureSkills PRIME portal; signing up alone does not help.
Freshers: build real projects and learn one area well, because firms now hire for skills, not for numbers.
Treat a job offer as firm only when you have a joining date in writing.
Call-centre staff: ask your employer about training for the difficult cases that chatbots cannot solve.
Check claims of mass layoffs or mass hiring against company results and trusted news before you act on them.

body: Language is where AI helps citizens most directly. Bhashini, the Government's language platform launched in 2022, offers translation and speech tools in 36 Indian languages for text and 22 for voice. Officials said in February 2026 that it had handled over 4 billion requests. In May 2026 the Government launched Samadhan Didi, a voice chatbot for the CPGRAMS complaints system. A person can speak a complaint in any of the 22 scheduled languages. The AI sorts it and sends it to the right department.

Courts use AI for typing and translation, not for deciding cases. The Supreme Court's SUVAS tool translates judgments into 18 Indian languages. AI also writes down spoken arguments in some Supreme Court hearings, with people checking the result. In Kerala, all trial courts have had to record witness statements with a speech-to-text tool called Adalat AI since November 2025. A Government note says another tool, SUPACE, meant to help judges with legal research, is still experimental and not in regular use.

Judges have also set limits. In July 2025 the Kerala High Court issued a policy for its district courts. It bars the use of AI tools to reach findings, orders or judgments, and bars feeding case details into unapproved AI tools. Any AI translation or legal citation must be checked by a person. The Supreme Court has an AI committee, headed by a sitting judge, that reviews pilot projects before wider use. The Government's stated position is that AI assists judges and does not replace their judgement.

Policing is the most disputed area. Delhi Police told the Supreme Court in August 2026 that face recognition had identified 2,873 people with criminal records at protests at Jantar Mantar. The Indian Express checked 205 of them who faced the most serious charges and found at least 25 were in jail at the time. Police say no action is taken on a match alone and that field checks follow. The Internet Freedom Foundation says no law clearly allows such scanning of crowds and wants it stopped.

For government staff, the change so far is in tasks more than in job numbers. ThePrint reported in October 2025 that court stenographers using AI typing tools were moved to correcting transcripts and uploading records, and that many had feared for their jobs. Officials need new skills too: the national AI guidelines call for training officers, regulators and police. There is no published official count of how many government posts in India have been cut or created because of AI.

The rules are still being built. The India AI Governance Guidelines, drawn up by a committee the IT ministry set up in July 2025, rest on seven principles and build on existing laws instead of a new AI law for now. The data protection law is only partly in force. Registration of consent managers opened in November 2026, but most duties on organisations and most rights of citizens start on 13 May 2027. Legal press reported in September 2026 that the Data Protection Board still had no members.
tips: Use Samadhan Didi or the CPGRAMS website to file a complaint in your own language, and keep the registration number.
If a translated court order matters to you, ask your lawyer to check it against the original.
If a government chatbot gives a wrong or unclear answer, ask to deal with an officer and keep a screenshot.
Before giving your face, fingerprint or ID to any office or app, ask why it is needed and how long it will be kept.
If a camera system wrongly identifies you, ask in writing how the match was made and get legal help.
Follow trusted news on the data protection law, because most of its protections begin in May 2027.

world.title: AI in India's factories and warehouses
world.summary: Indian plants use AI cameras, robots and smart maintenance, mostly at large firms. Small suppliers are behind, and the effect on shop-floor jobs has not been measured.

body: AI is already at work in some Indian plants, mainly to check quality and improve safety. At ABB India's factory at Nelamangala near Bengaluru, an AI camera photographs each finished circuit breaker from five sides and clears it for packing only if it passes every check. Tata Steel has shown AI that watches for unsafe acts on the shop floor and helps run parts of steel-making. Tata Motors has shown its own robots for moving materials. Most such reports come from the companies themselves and are not independently checked.

Robots are spreading, from a low base. The International Federation of Robotics says India installed almost 10,500 industrial robots in 2025, 15% more than the year before, making it the sixth-largest market. Car and auto-parts makers are the biggest buyers. In 2024 parts suppliers installed 2,100 robots, 40% more than a year earlier. Still, India has only about 30 robots for every 10,000 factory workers, against a world average of 132. Experts quoted by Business Today expect mixed factories of people and machines, not fully automatic ones.

Warehouses and delivery networks use AI to sort parcels and plan routes. Delhivery opened its mapping tools to other companies in June 2026. It says they are built on records of over 200 crore shipments and help with checking addresses, planning routes and estimating arrival times. Amazon already uses a system in India that scans and labels parcels before dispatch. Its robotics chief said in June 2026 that the company will expand robots and automation in its Indian warehouses.

Government support exists but is modest. The Ministry of Heavy Industries has set up four SAMARTH centres, in Pune, Delhi and Bengaluru, where firms can see smart-factory tools in use. The IT ministry and Nasscom run Centres of Excellence for AI that support start-ups building tools for manufacturers. Production-linked incentive schemes reward the making of advanced vehicles and batteries in India, though they are not AI schemes. The ministry has also approved projects with skill councils to create advanced skilling courses for the capital goods sector.

What does this mean for shop-floor workers? It has not been measured in India yet. Industry leaders quoted by Business Today say jobs will change, with workers moving to running, watching and repairing machines, and that tiring tasks such as visual inspection will be automated first. The same report describes a Noida firm comparing a robot with five workers who each cost about ₹1 lakh a month. Asked in Parliament in December 2025 about job losses from AI, the Labour Ministry listed training schemes and cited no study.

Small suppliers face the biggest hurdles. The research group ORF says small firms struggle to choose the right tools, pay for them and find skilled staff. Many tools assume good English, steady power and internet, and clean data. ORF warns that early spending can become a cost trap, and that AI could widen the gap between large and small firms. There is a wider limit too: most success stories so far come from company statements and events, not from independent studies of Indian plants.
tips: Workers: ask for training on any new machine or software, and learn basic machine maintenance and how to read its data.
Ask your ITI, employer or sector skill council which automation courses are open to you.
Small firms: start with one clear problem, such as rejected parts or machine stoppages, and test a tool before buying a large system.
Ask a SAMARTH centre or your industry association for a demonstration before you spend.
Ask vendors for proof from a plant like yours, not only a brochure.
Keep trained people in charge of safety decisions, even when an AI system gives alerts.

world.title: AI in India's films, music and news
world.summary: AI now copies actors' voices for dubbing and reads the news on some channels. Courts have protected stars' voices, and new rules say AI-made content must be labelled.

body: AI voices are now used in Indian cinema. In October 2026 the Tamil version of the film Bethlehem Kudumba Unit was released with actor Nivin Pauly's lines spoken in an AI copy of his voice. A Tamil dubbing artist performed the lines first. A company called Vaani then trained a copy of the actor's voice and placed it over that performance, a job it says took about two hours. The company said the reason was shortage of time, not cost, and that the voice copy was not kept afterwards.

AI has also been used to change finished films. In August 2025 the company Eros re-released the 2013 film Raanjhanaa in Tamil with a new, happy ending made with AI. In the original, the lead character dies. Actor Dhanush and director Aanand L Rai objected in public and said it was done without their agreement. Eros replied that the version was lawful, was labelled as an AI alternate, and did not replace the original. One lawyer notes that under copyright law the producer is the first owner of a film.

Courts have stepped in to protect well-known people. In 2024 the Bombay High Court, in a case brought by singer Arijit Singh, held that offering AI tools that turn any voice into a celebrity's voice without permission violates that person's rights. In 2025 the same court gave singer Asha Bhosle a temporary order against AI firms and online sellers. Actor Anil Kapoor won an order in the Delhi High Court in 2023. These are mostly temporary orders in single cases. India has no separate law on voice or likeness.

The Government has tightened rules for online platforms. Changes to the IT Rules took effect on 20 February 2026. Content made or altered by AI so that it looks real must carry a clear label, and platforms must add hidden markers that cannot be removed. Social media platforms must ask users to declare AI content before it is posted. Some lawful takedown orders must now be followed within three hours instead of 36. Routine editing and technical corrections are not covered by the labelling rules.

For workers, the picture is only partly measured. Voice artists told Deccan Chronicle in November 2026 that work is moving to cheaper AI voices. One member of the Association of Voice Artists said monthly projects fell from 15-20 to 6-7. In a 2026 survey of 254 screenwriters, 41% used AI tools at least sometimes, and 68% felt AI lowers the value of human creativity for producers. Channels such as Aaj Tak and Odisha TV have tried AI anchors. These are single accounts and small surveys, not national figures on jobs.

Big questions are still open. A Government panel proposed in December 2025 that AI firms get a blanket licence to train on copyrighted work and pay royalties through one collecting body. This is a proposal, not law. In July 2026 the Delhi High Court refused news agency ANI's request for a temporary order against OpenAI, and the main case continues. The labelling rules place duties on platforms but, as one lawyer notes, do not give performers a clear right over their own voice.
tips: Look for an 'AI-generated' label, and doubt any shocking clip of a famous person until trusted news confirms it.
Report fake or harmful AI content through the platform's complaint tool; platforms now have shorter deadlines to act.
Voice artists, singers and actors: read contracts for voice-cloning or AI clauses before signing, and ask how recordings will be used.
Writers and artists: keep dated drafts and records that show the work is yours.
Do not copy a real person's voice or face with AI unless you have clear permission.
If your own voice or face is misused, save the evidence and get advice from a lawyer or the police.

world.summary: AI cameras issue traffic fines, railway sensors warn of elephants on the track and airports check faces at the gate. Errors and privacy gaps are real.
