body: On city roads, AI mostly controls signals and catches violations. Bengaluru's adaptive signal system covers 169 junctions and changes signal timings using live traffic data. The firm that designed it claims travel time fell by up to 25%, a figure that has not been independently checked. The city's enforcement cameras read number plates and detect offences at 50 major junctions. On highways, the Dwarka Expressway and the Bengaluru-Mysuru road use AI video systems to detect accidents, stalled vehicles and speeding.

These cameras feed the e-challan system, and the Supreme Court wants more of them. In an order of 28 September 2026 it told states and highway bodies to make electronic enforcement AI-enabled. It noted that over ₹23,000 crore in e-challan fines was unpaid and ordered steps against defaulters. Vehicles with unpaid challans can be impounded, and services such as registration renewal and pollution certificates can be blocked until dues are cleared. It also told the road ministry to publish a public dashboard of enforcement data.

Indian Railways uses AI mainly for safety. An AI system using sound-sensing technology detects elephants near the track and warns loco pilots and station masters. It works on 141 route km in the Northeast, with contracts awarded for 981 km more. Video systems at 1,731 stations include AI alerts and face recognition. Railways is also testing AI to predict signal failures and to spot loose or missing parts on moving trains. Kavach, the automatic train protection system, is separate and covered over 2,200 route km by February 2026.

At airports, Digi Yatra lets passengers enter using a face scan instead of showing papers at each gate. The civil aviation ministry said in May 2026 that it had been used for over 10 crore journeys and would be extended to 27 more airports, making 65 in all. The Government has said its use is voluntary. In delivery, companies use AI to read unclear addresses and plan routes. Delhivery says its mapping tools draw on 100 crore GPS signals a day from over one lakh vehicles.

For transport workers, AI so far changes how work is guided and watched more than who is employed. Railway systems are built to alert and assist loco pilots, not to replace them. Bengaluru's traffic police say officers check AI-detected violations before a challan is issued. Delivery riders are directed by apps. More than 2 lakh riders stopped work on New Year's Eve 2025 over pay, safety and 10-minute delivery targets. There is no published Indian data yet on how many transport jobs AI has removed or created.

Accuracy and privacy are the main worries. In September 2026 a Bengaluru rider carrying a guitar was fined ₹500 because a camera took it for a passenger without a helmet. The challan was later cancelled. That month a car driver in Belagavi district got a no-helmet notice. With stricter penalties for unpaid challans, such errors matter more. On Digi Yatra, the Internet Freedom Foundation's founder says its data-deletion claims have had no outside audit, and that the RTI Act does not cover the body that runs it.
tips: Check your vehicle's challans on the official e-challan portal, and look at the photo before you pay.
If a challan is wrong, complain quickly to the traffic police or through the portal's grievance option, and keep proof.
Keep your number plate clean and readable, and report a stolen vehicle or a copied plate to the police at once.
Digi Yatra is optional: you can still use the regular entry lane with your ticket and ID.
Read an app's privacy policy before you give it your face or ID details.
Follow road signs and signals yourself; do not depend only on a navigation app.

world.title: Where India stands in the AI race today
world.summary: India is one of the biggest users of AI and now builds its own models, but they are still much smaller than the top US and Chinese ones. This page shows what exists, what is being built and what is missing.

body: India now has its own AI models. Sarvam AI of Bengaluru has a main model with 105 billion parameters, a rough measure of size, and speech models for 22 Indian languages. BharatGen, a government-funded group led by IIT Bombay, released Param 2 with 17 billion parameters in February 2026. Gnani.ai and Soket AI also have government support. AI4Bharat at IIT Madras helps build open speech and translation models. Ola's Krutrim closed its Kruti assistant in 2026 and now focuses on cloud services.

These models are far smaller than the world's leaders. GLM 5.2, an open Chinese model that Sarvam itself hosts, has 768 billion parameters, about seven times Sarvam's largest. In July 2026 Sarvam said it had about 2,000 of Nvidia's newest chips, planned to reach 10,000, and would finish a one-trillion-parameter model within six months. Its claim of beating smaller versions of GPT and Gemini comes from a test Sarvam built itself. No Indian model appears in the independent test data this app uses, so it cannot rank them.

The IndiaAI Mission is the Government's main AI plan. The Cabinet approved it in March 2024 with ₹10,372 crore for five years. It does not own chips. It rents time on more than 38,000 GPUs from private cloud firms and pays part of the bill, so users pay about ₹65 an hour. By October 2026 it had committed ₹1,275 crore in subsidies. ThePrint found ₹1,058 crore went to nine model builders and about ₹10 crore to researchers and students. AIKosh lists over 16,000 datasets.

Data centres and chip plants are being built, but the hardest parts are still ahead. India had about 1.6 to 1.8 gigawatts of data centre capacity in late 2026, and one report expects this to double within two years. Google plans a 15 billion dollar hub in Visakhapatnam. Twelve chip projects are approved. Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi have begun commercial production in Sanand, Gujarat. The large Tata chip-making plant at Dholera is now expected in mid-2028, and it will start with older 90-nanometre technology.

India has real strengths. Stanford's 2026 AI Index counted 50,460 AI researchers and inventors in India, second only to the United States, and gave India the world's highest score for AI skills. More than 80% of Indian employees in its survey said they use AI at work, against 58% worldwide. India's many languages give local builders a clear task, and AI4Bharat shares its datasets and models openly. The Government's Bhashini platform offers speech and translation tools. Aadhaar and UPI show that India can build public digital systems at large scale.

The gaps are just as real. India spends 0.64% of its GDP on research, against 2.43% in China and 3.48% in the United States. Private AI investment in India was about 4 billion dollars in 2025, against about 285 billion in the US. India also had the largest net outflow of AI talent among countries tracked. Researchers told ThePrint that university labs can wait months for computing time. India is a large user of AI and a serious builder of language tools, but not yet a maker of top-end models.
tips: Treat a claim that an Indian or foreign model 'beats' another as a company claim until an independent test confirms it.
When you read big numbers about GPUs, data centres or investment, check whether they are plans or things already built.
Students, researchers and start-ups can apply for low-cost GPU time through the IndiaAI Compute Portal.
Developers can look for Indian-language datasets and models on AIKosh before paying for data.
Watch two dates: the one-trillion-parameter Indian models promised for early 2027, and the Dholera chip plant in 2028.

world.title: India's AI rules and your rights
world.summary: India has no single AI law. A mix of guidelines, IT rules on deepfakes, a data protection law and regulator advice applies, and some parts have not started yet. This page shows what is in force and where you can complain today.

body: India has no single AI law. In November 2025 the IT Ministry released the India AI Governance Guidelines. They set seven guiding principles, including trust, people first, fairness and accountability, and they prefer using existing laws where possible. They are guidance, not binding rules. In April 2026 the Government set up a group of ministries, chaired by IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, to coordinate AI policy, with an expert committee to advise it. Regulators such as RBI, SEBI and the Data Protection Board are not members of that group.

The clearest binding rules are about fake photos, videos and voices. Since 20 February 2026 the IT rules cover 'synthetically generated information': audio, images or video made or changed by a computer to look real. AI-written text is not covered. Platforms must label such content, and large social media platforms must ask users to declare it. A platform must act on a court or government order within three hours. Complaints about nude, sexual or morphed images must be acted on within two hours, and general complaints within seven days.

More changes may come. In March and April 2026 the Ministry published draft amendments. One would make the AI label stay visible for the full length of a video. Others would require platforms to follow Ministry advisories and would extend government oversight to news shared by users. Press bodies, including the Editors Guild of India, asked for the draft to be withdrawn. A law-firm tracker dated September 2026 still listed it as a draft. In June 2026 the Supreme Court published draft rules on how courts may use AI.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 covers how companies, including AI firms, use your personal data. Its rules were notified in November 2025 and start in steps. The rule on registering consent managers took effect on 13 November 2026. The main duties start on 13 May 2027: notices, consent, data safety, reporting of data leaks, children's data and your rights over your data. Penalties go up to ₹250 crore. The Data Protection Board exists on paper, but by mid-November 2026 reports said no members had been appointed.

Financial regulators have spoken too. An RBI committee report of August 2025, called FREE-AI, made 26 recommendations for safe AI in finance. It is guidance, not a binding rule. In August 2026 RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said a bank cannot blame a model for a wrong decision, and asked banks for board-approved AI policies and real human oversight. SEBI rules in force since 2025 make regulated firms responsible for the AI tools they use. In November 2026 the SEBI chairman said detailed AI guidelines for markets would be issued soon.

What can you do today? For a deepfake or fake profile, report it in the app and to the platform's grievance officer. If you are not satisfied, appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee at gac.gov.in within 30 days. For online fraud, call 1930 or file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in. For a bank or other RBI-regulated lender, use the RBI portal cms.rbi.org.in or call 14448. For brokers and listed companies, complain to the firm first, then use SEBI's SCORES portal. For misuse of your data, write to the company's grievance officer.
tips: Save proof before you complain: screenshots, links, dates and the name of the account.
Report nude, sexual or morphed images to the platform at once; the rules give it two hours to act.
After any money fraud, call 1930 as early as you can, then file the complaint at cybercrime.gov.in.
If a platform ignores or rejects your complaint, appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee within 30 days.
Look for an 'AI-generated' label, but do not trust a photo or video only because it has no label.
Before you give personal data to an AI app, check who runs it and how to reach its grievance officer.

world.title: AI and jobs: what the evidence says
world.summary: AI is changing many jobs, but so far the clearest damage is fewer entry-level openings, not mass job loss.

stats.label: Jobs worldwide with tasks exposed to generative AI (estimate)
stats.source: International Labour Organization (ILO)

stats.label: Job shortfall for US 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed work (measured)
stats.source: Stanford Digital Economy Lab

stats.label: Announced US job cuts in 2026 that employers blamed on AI
stats.source: Challenger, Gray & Christmas via HCAMag

body: Big forecasts come first. A World Economic Forum survey of over 1,000 employers, published in January 2025, predicts that 170 million jobs will be created and 92 million lost by 2030. That would leave 78 million more jobs overall. This is a forecast, not a measurement, and AI is only one of the causes it covers.

Being exposed to AI is not the same as losing your job. The ILO estimates about one in four jobs worldwide has tasks AI could do, rising to 34% in rich countries. Office and clerical work is the most exposed. In rich countries, women are more likely than men to hold the most exposed jobs. The ILO says most jobs are likely to change rather than vanish. The IMF says about 40% of jobs worldwide, and 60% in rich economies, will be affected in some way.

What has actually happened so far? Stanford's 2026 AI Index says big job losses have not yet shown up in overall employment figures, even though 88% of surveyed organisations use AI. US Census data show about one in five US businesses used AI in spring 2026. In the US, employers named AI as the reason for 121,401 announced job cuts from January to October 2026. That is more than double the 2025 total. But these are reasons companies give, and some experts think AI is sometimes used as an excuse.

Young people starting out are feeling it most. Payroll data studied at Stanford show that 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs, such as software and customer service, are about 19% below where they would be otherwise. The gap was 15% a year earlier. It mostly comes from fewer new hires, not firings, and older workers in the same jobs show no gap. The researchers say this is a warning sign, not final proof that AI is the cause.

Jobs where AI helps people, rather than replacing them, are holding steady or growing. Employers expect demand to grow for AI and data specialists, and also for care workers, teachers, farm workers and drivers. Cashiers, office assistants and graphic designers are among the jobs expected to shrink. Employers expect nearly 40% of the skills used at work to change by 2030. Most say they will retrain staff, but 41% also plan to cut jobs where AI can do the tasks.
tips: List the tasks in your job and spot which ones are routine and could be automated.
Practise using AI tools at work so you become the person who checks and guides them.
Build skills AI finds hard, like dealing with people, judgement and hands-on work.
If you are starting out, gather real experience early through projects, internships or volunteering.

world.summary: AI is helping doctors read scans and write notes, but the gains are often modest and health chatbots can get things wrong.

body: AI is already part of everyday medicine. The US medicines regulator has cleared more than 1,600 AI-enabled devices, for jobs like spotting eye disease caused by diabetes or checking skin images for cancer. In an American Medical Association survey of nearly 1,700 doctors in early 2026, 81% said they use AI, up from 38% in 2023. Common uses are summarising research and drafting notes and care plans.

Some of the strongest evidence comes from breast cancer screening. A Swedish trial with more than 100,000 women, published in The Lancet in January 2026, tested AI that helps doctors read mammograms. The AI group had 12% fewer cancers turning up between screenings, and false alarms stayed about the same. Earlier results from the same trial showed radiologists had 44% less reading work. The study used one AI system in one country, so results may differ elsewhere.

AI 'scribes' listen to appointments and draft the doctor's notes. A large 2026 study in JAMA followed more than 1,800 clinicians at five US hospitals. Those using scribes spent about 16 fewer minutes a day on notes. That is helpful but modest, and the authors say it may not be enough to explain why some doctors feel less burnt out.

There are real risks. A study in BMJ Open, reported in April 2026, tested five popular chatbots on health questions. About half the answers had problems and almost 20% were seriously misleading. Doctors also worry: 88% fear that relying on AI could weaken medical skills, especially for young doctors, and 27% have had no AI training. Privacy of patient data is another concern.

Expect more AI behind the scenes, from booking to scans to paperwork, with doctors still making the final call. Doctors say they want clear rules on who is responsible when AI makes a mistake. In the EU, stricter rules for high-risk AI built into products such as medical devices have been pushed back to August 2028.
tips: Use chatbots to prepare questions for your doctor, not to diagnose yourself.
In an emergency, call a doctor or emergency number instead of asking a chatbot.
It is fine to ask your clinic if AI is used in your care and how your data is kept.
Check any health claim from AI against a trusted source like your national health service.

body: Finance was an early adopter. In a 2024 survey by the Bank of England and the UK regulator, 75% of firms said they use AI, including 95% of insurers. Firms said the biggest benefits are spotting fraud and money laundering, cybersecurity and analysing data. In the US, about a third of finance and insurance businesses reported using AI in spring 2026. Barclays, for example, has used AI to summarise more than 8 million customer calls.

Jobs are being cut, but it is hard to say how many cuts are caused by AI. The New York Times reported in April 2026 that six of the largest US banks shed about 15,000 staff while their profits rose 18%. Citi has pledged to cut 20,000 jobs. In insurance, Allianz Partners said in July 2026 it will cut 1,500 to 1,800 jobs in Europe because of AI, mostly where staff handle claims and questions by phone.

Junior roles are the most affected. A McKinsey expert told Fortune that some banks are cutting their junior analyst intake by up to two-thirds. A lawyer warned this could hit women harder, as many junior office roles are held by women. Some firms have also gone too far. Klarna said in 2024 its AI assistant did the work of 700 support staff, but in 2025 its boss admitted quality had suffered and it began hiring humans again.

Criminals use AI too. In one 2024 case, a worker in Hong Kong sent $25 million to fraudsters after a video call with fake, AI-made versions of her bosses. Deloitte forecasts that fraud losses enabled by generative AI in the US could reach $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023. Regulators also worry that firms do not fully understand their tools: 46% of UK firms said they only partly understand the AI they use.

Expect more AI chat assistants in banking apps, faster claims and loan decisions, and an arms race between fraudsters and fraud fighters. Fewer people may be hired into entry-level finance jobs. Regulators are watching for unfair decisions, data misuse and over-reliance on a few big tech suppliers.
tips: Never send money after an urgent call or video, even from a familiar face, without calling back on a number you know.
Agree a secret code word with family to check it is really them.
If a bank chatbot cannot help, ask to speak to a human.
If you are refused a loan or claim, ask the firm to explain the reasons.

world.summary: Nearly all students now use AI, and research shows it helps learning only when it is used like a tutor, not a shortcut.

body: AI has become normal in education. A UK survey of over 1,000 university students, published in March 2026, found 95% use AI and 94% use it for assessed work. Fewer than half felt well supported by their teachers in using it. In the US, 59% of school educators used AI tools in 2025-26, often to plan lessons, make worksheets and tests, and give feedback.

Some countries are rolling it out on purpose. Estonia's AI Leap programme began in September 2025 with 20,000 high school students and 3,000 teachers. It plans to add 38,000 more students from September 2026. Among US educators who use AI, 64% say it frees up time for the parts of teaching they care about most.

But getting a task done with AI is not the same as learning. The OECD's 2026 review of research found that students using general chatbots often produce better work, but the advantage can vanish in exams without AI. In a trial with nearly 1,000 maths students in Turkey, those using a plain chatbot did 48% better in practice but 17% worse in the exam. A version built to give hints instead of answers caused no harm in the exam.

Teachers worry about cheating. In OECD survey data, 72% of lower secondary teachers said AI can harm honesty by letting students pass off work as their own. Students worry too, about losing independent thinking and about being wrongly accused of cheating.

Expect more tutor-style AI tools that ask questions instead of giving answers, and more tests done in class or out loud. The OECD advises building core skills without AI first, then adding it with care. In the EU, strict rules for high-risk AI in education, such as AI used in exams or grading, have been delayed to December 2027.
tips: Try the task yourself first, then use AI to check your work or explain what you got wrong.
Ask AI to quiz you or give hints instead of writing the answer for you.
Learn your school's rules on AI and say when you have used it.
Double-check facts and sources from AI, because it can make things up.

body: Software is where AI has moved fastest. In April 2026, Google's boss said 75% of the company's new code is made by AI and then approved by engineers, up from about half in late 2025. That is the company's own claim and is hard to check. Engineers increasingly supervise AI 'agents' that write and change code, rather than typing every line.

Most developers use these tools, but many are wary. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey of over 49,000 developers, 84% use or plan to use AI and about half of professionals use it daily. Only about a third trust its accuracy, and 46% distrust it. The top complaint, named by 66%, is answers that are almost right but not quite.

Does AI really make coders faster? The evidence is mixed. A careful 2025 trial by the research group METR found experienced developers took 19% longer with AI, even though they felt faster. A late-2025 follow-up hinted at speed-ups, but METR says that data is unreliable. Company surveys collected by Stanford report gains of around 26%.

Jobs are shifting, especially for beginners. Stanford's AI Index says employment of software developers aged 22 to 25 fell nearly 20% from 2024. US job ads for software developers are still 27.5% below early 2020, though they have risen about 15% since early 2025. Most of that rise is for senior roles, and over a third is for jobs with AI in the title.

The risks include hidden bugs, security holes and people trusting code they do not understand. Expect smaller teams, more work checking and testing AI's output, and strong demand for people who can design systems and guide AI well. The worry is that if fewer juniors are hired, there will be fewer experienced developers later.
tips: Learn the basics of coding properly, so you can tell when AI output is wrong.
Always read, test and understand AI-written code before using it.
Never paste passwords, keys or private company data into public AI tools.
Build a portfolio of projects that shows you can use AI tools responsibly.

body: AI-made content is flooding in. The music service Deezer says fully AI-made tracks passed half of its new daily uploads in June 2026. Yet they make up only 1-3% of what people actually listen to, and Deezer says up to 85% of plays on such tracks in 2025 were fake, used to cheat on royalties. Deezer now labels AI music and keeps it out of its recommendations.

Some creative workers are losing paid work. In a 2026 survey of 549 UK illustrators, 46% said they knew a client had chosen AI over them, up from 32% a year before. More than half said their income fell, though the economy may also play a part. In the Netherlands, one in five freelance artists reported losing income to AI, and about a third of translators. The World Economic Forum lists graphic designers among the fastest-shrinking jobs.

The biggest fight is over copyright: can AI firms train on people's work without paying? In the US, a judge said training on books can be legal, but downloading pirated copies was not. That led AI company Anthropic to agree a $1.5 billion settlement with authors, about $3,000 per book, approved in July 2026. In the UK, the High Court ruled in late 2025 that Stability AI's image model does not store copies of Getty's photos, rejecting Getty's main remaining copyright claim. Getty has been allowed to appeal.

Many fights are still open. Disney and Universal sued the image tool Midjourney in June 2025, saying it copies characters like Darth Vader. In music, Universal and Warner settled with AI song tool Udio, and Warner settled with Suno in late 2025. These deals come with licences, so artists' music can be used in return for payment.

AI also helps creators, for example by speeding up editing, translation and early sketches, and by letting small creators make things on a tiny budget. Next, expect more licensing deals and clearer labels. In the EU, AI chatbots must say they are AI, and deepfakes must be labelled, from August 2026. Hidden digital markers on AI content are required for existing tools by December 2026.
tips: Look for 'AI-generated' labels and be sceptical of viral images, videos or songs.
If you create things, read contracts and platform settings on whether your work can train AI.
Support human artists you like by buying, crediting and sharing their work directly.
Use AI as a starting point for ideas, then add your own voice and checks.

world.title: AI data centres: the giant buildings behind AI
world.summary: AI runs in huge, power-hungry buildings, and the rush to build more is changing power grids, water use and nearby towns.

body: A data centre is a big building full of computers called servers. AI data centres are packed with special chips that train and run tools like chatbots. They need a lot of electricity, plus cooling so the chips do not overheat. The IEA says one AI-focused data centre can use as much power as 100,000 homes, and the biggest ones being built will use about 20 times more.

The US is far ahead. Stanford's 2026 AI Index counts 5,427 US data centres, more than ten times any other country. In 2024 the US used about 45% of all data centre electricity, China about 25% and Europe about 15%, says the IEA. China had about 32 gigawatts (GW) of data centre capacity at the end of 2025 and could reach about 60 GW by 2030, according to Rystad Energy, with much of it in western regions where land and power are cheaper.

Other regions are racing to catch up. In Abu Dhabi, the first 200 megawatt (MW) part of the Stargate UAE campus was due in the third quarter of 2026, as step one of a planned 5 GW site. In India, Google plans to invest about $15 billion from 2026 to 2030 in an AI hub in Visakhapatnam. The EU has opened bidding for up to seven 'AI gigafactories', with more than €30 billion of public and private money expected. Winners are due in early 2027.

The biggest sites are in the US. Research group Epoch AI estimates that Amazon's campus in New Carlisle, Indiana, built for Anthropic, runs about 1,037 MW of computer power, xAI's Colossus 2 in Memphis about 946 MW, and OpenAI's Stargate site in Abilene, Texas about 824 MW. Meta says its Hyperion campus in Louisiana will grow to 5 GW, with more than $50 billion invested. The IEA says five big tech firms spent over $400 billion on buildings and equipment in 2025 and expects about 75% more in 2026. Not all of this is AI, and not every announced project will be built.

The IEA measured a 17% rise in data centre electricity use in 2025, and about 50% for AI-focused ones. It forecasts use will roughly double to about 950 TWh by 2030, around 3% of the world's electricity. Water is harder to pin down. The IEA estimated about 560 billion litres in 2023, counting cooling plus water used to make power and chips, rising to about 1,200 billion litres by 2030. Other studies give very different numbers because they count water in different ways.

Neighbours feel the effects. In a large US power grid region that covers Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland, the market's independent watchdog said data centre demand was the main reason power capacity prices hit records. Maryland's consumer advocate estimated one auction added from under $1 to about $5 a month to many home bills. Data Center Watch counted at least 75 US projects worth about $130 billion blocked or delayed by local opposition in early 2026, over power, water and land. Towns can gain jobs and taxes: Meta expects over 1,000 permanent jobs in Louisiana, but critics worry households may pay some costs later. Expect more building, but slower than promised, as the IEA says shortages of turbines, transformers and grid connections are holding projects back.
tips: If a data centre is planned near you, follow your local council or planning meetings, where deals on water, noise and power are often made.
Check your electricity bill for new capacity or transmission charges, and ask your power company what is driving them.

world.summary: Factories and warehouses are adding robots and AI faster than ever, but most companies are still testing rather than using it everywhere.

body: Factories have used robots for decades. Old-style robot arms repeat the same welding or painting steps again and again. What is new is AI: cameras and software that let machines spot faulty parts, warn before a machine breaks and adjust to changes. The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) counted more than 600,000 new industrial robots installed in 2025, up 11%, bringing the world total to about 5 million.

China dominates. It installed 354,000 robots in 2025, 59% of the world total, and Chinese makers supplied more than half of them. The US came second with about 38,500, overtaking Japan. The IFR forecasts about 655,000 new installations in 2026, a rise of 9%.

Warehouses are changing fast too. Amazon said in mid-2025 that it had deployed its one millionth robot and that robots help with about 75% of its customer orders. It uses an AI model called DeepFleet to steer its robots and expects it to cut robot travel time by about 10%, a company estimate. Human-shaped robots are still being tested, not rolled out widely. In a two-week trial at a Siemens factory in Germany in January 2026, one moved about 60 boxes an hour with over 90% success, according to the companies' own figures.

AI software also helps plan supply chains, predict demand and check quality. In a survey of 1,200 manufacturing leaders by software firm Parsec, done in February 2026, 72% said they used AI in some way, up from 53% in 2024. But only 10% used it across their whole operations. Quality control (50%) and supply chain management (45%) were top uses. The biggest barriers were cost, data security and trouble linking AI to older systems.

The benefits can be real: fewer faulty products, less downtime, and robots taking on heavy or dangerous work. The downsides include fewer jobs for some routine tasks, pressure on workers to learn new skills, and expensive projects that never pay off. Amazon says it has trained more than 700,000 staff in new skills since 2019, but that is the company's own claim.

Over the next year or two, expect more robots, especially in China, and more AI cameras and planning tools in factories. Human-shaped robots will mostly stay in trials. The big question is whether companies move from small tests to everyday use.
tips: If you work in a factory or warehouse, ask whether your employer offers training on the new machines and software.
Be careful with viral videos of humanoid robots: many show short demos or trials, not everyday work.

body: Many people now ask chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini for gift ideas or to compare products. Adobe, which measures traffic to US shopping websites, found that visits coming from AI tools rose about 693% in the 2025 holiday season compared with a year earlier. Adobe says the number of people doing this is still modest. Shoppers mostly used AI to find deals and research products.

Buying inside a chatbot has had a bumpy start. In late 2025 OpenAI launched Instant Checkout so people could buy from Walmart and other shops without leaving ChatGPT. Walmart later said purchases made inside the chatbot happened about three times less often than when shoppers were sent to its own website. In March 2026 it switched to putting its own shopping assistant, Sparky, inside ChatGPT instead. For now, AI helps people research, but most buying still happens on shops' own sites and apps.

Customer service is where AI is spreading fastest. In a Gartner survey of 3,566 customers in early 2026, half said AI made dealing with companies easier. But 87% said companies using AI must offer a way to reach a human. People were about three times more likely to use outside tools like ChatGPT than a company's own chatbot to sort out a problem.

Fears of mass job losses in call centres have not come true yet. In a Gartner survey of 275 service leaders in mid-2026, only 21% said they had cut human agent numbers because of AI. Where cuts happened, they averaged about 17% of staff. Some firms went too far: 7% had already rehired people after cuts, and 11% planned to.

The benefits are faster answers at any hour and easier price comparison. The risks include chatbots that trap you in loops, wrong answers given with confidence, and recommendations where it is not clear why one product is suggested over another. Shops also collect a lot of data about what you search and buy.

Over the next year or two, expect more AI assistants inside shopping apps and chatbots, and more AI help on phone lines. Gartner advises companies not to force every customer through AI first, so look for firms that keep a clear path to a person.

If a service chatbot cannot help, try typing 'agent' or 'human', which often passes you to a person.

body: Lawyers use AI to search past cases, summarise long documents and draft letters. In a survey of more than 1,300 legal professionals in late 2025, 69% said they used generative AI for work, up from 31% a year before. Firms are lagging behind their staff: only 9% had a written AI policy that is enforced, and 54% offered no training on safe use.

The biggest problem in court is made-up material. AI can invent cases that do not exist, and people have filed them. By the start of June 2026, a public database kept by researcher Damien Charlotin listed 1,058 US cases where AI misuse showed up in court filings. About 60% involved people representing themselves, not lawyers. A 2025 study found even specialist legal research tools gave wrong or invented answers 17% to 33% of the time.

Courts are responding. In May 2026 Florida's Supreme Court changed its rules so filings must confirm that cited cases exist and are quoted correctly. In England and Wales, guidance for judges updated in October 2025 warns them not to put private information into public AI tools and says judges stay personally responsible for anything issued in their name.

Governments are using more AI too. US federal agencies reported 3,611 AI uses in 2025, about double the 1,757 reported for 2024, and 445 were marked high-impact, such as summarising patients' medical records. In the UK, a government tool called Consult sorted more than 50,000 responses to a public consultation in about two hours, for £240 of computing plus 22 hours of expert checking. It agreed with human experts about 83% of the time. The government estimates it could save 75,000 days of staff time a year, which is a forecast, not a result.

Mistakes can be costly and embarrassing. Deloitte repaid part of an A$440,000 fee to the Australian government after a report it wrote with AI help was found to contain fake references and an invented quote from a court ruling. Other worries include bias, privacy, and who is accountable when AI helps decide on benefits, policing or immigration.

Done well, AI could make paperwork faster, cut the cost of legal help and speed up public services. Over the next year or two, expect more rules that require people to disclose and check AI use, more penalties for fake citations, and more government chat assistants.
tips: If you use AI for a legal problem, check every law or case it mentions on an official website, or ask a qualified adviser.
Never paste private details such as ID numbers or medical records into a public chatbot.
If a government decision affects you, you can ask whether AI was used and how to appeal.

body: On farms, AI usually means cameras, sensors, satellites and software that help decide when to plant, water, spray or harvest. Examples include sprayers that spot weeds, drones that spray crops, phone apps that identify plant diseases and chatbots that answer farming questions.

Smart sprayers are one of the clearest examples. John Deere's See & Spray uses cameras and AI to spray only the weeds, not the whole field. Deere says farmers used it on more than five million acres in 2025 and cut their use of some weedkillers by nearly half on average, saving almost 31 million gallons of spray mix. These are company figures from customer data, not an independent trial.

Drones are spreading fastest in China. News site CleanTechnica estimates China had about 309,000 crop-spraying drones going into 2026 and that they carried out about 203 million hectares of spraying work in 2025. A field sprayed three times counts three times, and countries report this differently, so treat the numbers as rough.

Chatbots are reaching farmers too. McKinsey surveyed 5,500 farmers in ten countries in 2026. It found 17% use generative AI for farm tasks, but only 4% pay for it. Use is highest in Latin America and North America. Farmers are being careful with money because of economic pressure, and many still lean on trusted advisers when deciding what to buy.

The benefits can include using fewer chemicals, less water and fuel, and coping with labour shortages. The risks include high costs that favour big farms, questions over who owns a farm's data, poor internet in rural areas, and bad advice if an AI tool gets it wrong. Over the next year or two, expect more AI advice through phones and machines, but farmers will mostly buy what has proven results in local conditions.
tips: If you garden, plant-identification apps can suggest what is wrong with a plant, but check with a local expert before using any chemicals.
Farmers: ask sellers for independent trial results, not just company figures, and read who owns the data your machines collect.

world.title: AI in the next one to two years
world.summary: AI labs predict big leaps very soon, forecasters are split, and sceptics warn of hype, so here is the full range of views.

body: AI agents are tools that carry out tasks for you, such as filling in forms, booking things or writing and testing code. Research group METR found that the length of tasks top AI could finish, at least half the time, doubled about every seven months up to early 2025. It measured GPT-5 handling tasks that take a skilled person about 2 hours. Gartner forecasts that over 40% of company agent projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of cost, unclear value or weak safety controls.

Robots and gadgets are changing more slowly. The International Federation of Robotics expects about 655,000 new factory robots in 2026, up 9%, while human-shaped robots are still mostly in short trials. AI is moving into glasses and phones: Meta's Ray-Ban Display glasses, launched in September 2025 at $799, show messages, directions and live captions in the lens and are controlled by a wristband that reads muscle signals. Expect more assistants that can see what your camera sees, and more arguments about the privacy of people being filmed.

AI already helps science. The creators of AlphaFold, which predicts the shapes of proteins, shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and the tool has been used by over 2 million researchers in 190 countries. OpenAI said in November 2025 it expects AI to make very small discoveries in 2026 and bigger ones from 2028, while admitting it could be wrong. New medicines usually need years of testing, so even fast AI discoveries will take time to reach patients.

AGI, or artificial general intelligence, usually means AI that can do most thinking work as well as people, but there is no agreed definition. The fastest predictions come from the labs and their circle. Anthropic told the US government in March 2025 it expects very powerful AI, with top-expert skills in many fields, by late 2026 or early 2027. In November 2026 the AI Futures Project, which wrote the AI 2027 scenario, said it now expects AI able to do the work of top AI researchers some time in 2027. It gives a 35% to 65% chance that AI beats top experts at most tasks before 2028, while calling parts of its evidence preliminary.

Others are more cautious. On forecasting site Metaculus, the combined guess of about 1,900 forecasters for the first general AI was June 2030 as of November 2026. Sceptics point to an MIT study from 2025 that found about 95% of company generative AI pilots it examined had no measurable effect on profits. They also note that the best AI model still reads an analogue clock correctly only about half the time. Critic Gary Marcus argues the AI boom is a financial bubble. It is also worth remembering that AI companies benefit when people believe big predictions.

The safest bet for the next year or two is uneven progress: AI that is brilliant at some tasks and unreliable at others. Watch for real evidence, such as changes in jobs and prices, working products you can buy, and new laws, rather than bold promises.
tips: Treat dated predictions about AGI as informed guesses, and ask whether the person making them gains from the hype.
Try new AI agent features on low-risk tasks first, and check their work before trusting them with money or important messages.
Before buying camera glasses, think about the privacy of people around you and check local rules on recording.

world.title: What people think and want from AI
world.summary: People around the world use AI more and more, but many worry about it, trust is low and most want strong safety rules.

stats.label: Americans more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, 2025
stats.source: Pew Research Center

stats.label: People across 47 countries who say AI regulation is needed
stats.source: KPMG and University of Melbourne

stats.label: Americans who want AI safety rules kept even if development slows
stats.source: Gallup

body: Most people have mixed feelings. Pew Research surveyed 25 countries in 2025. Across them, the typical share who felt more worried than excited about AI was 34%, while 16% were more excited and 42% felt both equally. In no country were more than 30% mainly excited. Stanford's 2026 AI Index found 59% of people worldwide think AI products bring more benefits than drawbacks, up from 55% in 2024, but 52% say AI makes them nervous.

Views differ a lot by country. About half of adults in the US, Italy, Australia, Brazil and Greece are mainly worried, compared with as few as 16% in South Korea. Optimism is highest in Southeast Asia: over 80% in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore expect AI to change their lives a lot within three to five years. Trust in your own country to regulate AI ranges from 89% in India and 74% in Indonesia to 22% in Greece, with the US at 44%. Across countries, more people trust the EU (53%) to regulate AI well than the US (37%) or China (27%).

Use is rising faster than trust. KPMG and the University of Melbourne surveyed more than 48,000 people in 47 countries in late 2024 and early 2025. They found 66% use AI regularly, but only 46% are willing to trust it, and 56% say they have made mistakes at work because of AI. In a 2025 Gallup poll, only 2% of Americans fully trusted AI to make fair, unbiased decisions, and 29% trusted it somewhat.

People welcome some uses and reject others. In Pew's June 2025 US survey, most were happy for AI to play a role in weather forecasting (74%), spotting financial crime (70%), finding benefit fraud (70%) and developing new medicines (66%). About two-thirds said AI should have no role in judging whether two people could fall in love, and 73% said it should not advise people about faith. Over half (53%) think AI will make people worse at creative thinking. Three in four say it is very important to know whether content was made by AI, but 53% are not confident they could tell.

Most people want rules. In the KPMG study, 70% said AI regulation is needed. In the Gallup poll, 80% of Americans wanted safety and data rules kept even if that slows AI development, and 72% wanted independent experts to test AI before release. About six in ten Americans want more control over how AI is used in their own lives, says Pew.

There is also a big gap between experts and the public. In the US, 73% of AI experts expect AI to have a positive effect on jobs, compared with 23% of the public, according to the AI Index. Expect this debate to shape new laws over the next year or two.
tips: Look for labels that say whether a picture, video or text was made by AI, and be extra careful when there is no label.
Check your apps' settings to see whether your chats are used to train AI, and switch it off if you prefer.
Tell your elected representatives what AI rules you want, because public opinion helps shape new laws.
